<description>
{
 "summary": "Restricts descriptor expansion in `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::TopUpWithDB()` to start at `range_start` instead of index 0, and records the derived index directly rather than incrementing an offset from -1. Also aligns `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::Load()` to set `m_max_cached_index` to the actual index loaded.",
 "problem": "When importing a descriptor with range `[N, M]`, the wallet expands and tracks keys starting from index 0 instead of `N`. This causes import times to scale with M rather than the range size M - N, falsely treats scriptPubKeys below N as `IsMine` until wallet restart (causing rescanned transactions below N to lose ownership on reload), can trigger derivation of up to 2^31 keys for high range starts, and causes redundant re-expansions on active wallet reload due to miscalculated `m_max_cached_index`.",
 "evidence": [
  "Author benchmark: 'Importing wpkh(xpub/0/*) with \"range\": [600000, 600009] into a blank watch-only wallet goes from 19.5s to 0.09s on this machine.' (PR description)",
  "Author notes vulnerability to excessive derivation: 'Since ParseDescriptorRange() only bounds the size of the range and not its start, \"range\": [2146483648, 2147483647] is accepted and expands 2^31 indexes into m_map_script_pub_keys before the RPC returns.' (PR description)"
 ],

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
